did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 17 opens with the heading “A Prayer of David.” At its opening, David asks the LORD to listen to his prayer and examine his claim to justice, emphasizing that his words are not spoken with deceit.
Did you know? David describes the testing of his heart at night: “You have visited me by night.” The night serves here as a time of examination and reflection, not merely as a designation of time.

Did you know? David connects his faithfulness to the LORD’s ways with the way people behave: “Concerning the deeds of men, by the word of your lips.” The LORD’s words are presented as a compass that enables him to avoid “the paths of the violent.”

Did you know? The chapter features a central image of a path: David asks the LORD to support his steps in “your paths,” so that his feet may not slip. The path here symbolizes stability and faithfulness.

Did you know? David asks the LORD to “show the wonders of your steadfast love”—that is, to reveal His love in a special way—and calls Him “the Savior of those who take refuge in You,” emphasizing the protection given to those who trust in Him.

Did you know? Divine protection is described through two powerful images: being kept “as the apple of the eye” and sheltered “under the shadow of your wings.” Both express closeness, tenderness, and protection from danger.

Did you know? The description of the enemies combines physical and verbal imagery: “They have closed their hearts” portrays their hardness and pride, while “their mouths speak arrogantly” presents their speech as haughty.
Did you know? The enemies are compared to a lion and a young lion lying in wait for prey. The image emphasizes their danger, their strength, and the fact that they act from ambush.

Did you know? David distinguishes between the people of the world, whose portion is in this life and whose children inherit their possessions, and the hope expressed in the following verse—a satisfaction that does not depend solely on material abundance.

Did you know? The chapter concludes with the height of David’s hope: “As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness.” After describing his enemies and the dangers he faces, the prayer ends with a longing to see the LORD’s face and be satisfied by His presence.
